story: Gov. Mike Dunleavy signed the non binding White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge governors addendum on 2026-07-23, and the only Alaska utility on the pledge's signatory list is Cordova Electric Cooperative, a 1,566 customer island co op with 18 MW of generation that is not connected by transmission line to any other community, while every Railbelt utility that would actually serve a data center is absent and every state instrument that could make the promise binding is dead or unverifiable.

claims.claim: Gov. Mike Dunleavy of Alaska is one of 23 Republican governors who signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge addendum announced on July 23, 2026
claims.verbatim: Governor Kay Ivey (AL), Governor Mike Dunleavy (AK), Governor Sarah Sanders (AR), Governor Brian Kemp (GA), Governor Brad Little (ID)
claims.notes: Full 23 name list rendered on the page. Count and Dunleavy inclusion independently corroborated by USA TODAY and by the White House page counter reading 23 Governors.

claims.claim: The governors addendum commits signers to implement the principles established in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to the greatest extent possible in their respective positions
claims.verbatim: implement the principles established in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, to the greatest extent possible in our respective positions.
claims.source_outlet: USA TODAY via Central Oregon Daily
claims.notes: USA TODAY byline Joey Garrison. The RGA page quotes only the pledge preamble and does not reproduce the addendum wording, so this rests on the wire story. Attribute in slide copy as reported by USA TODAY.

claims.claim: The pledge is explicitly non binding
claims.verbatim: Although non-binding, the pledge includes an addendum for the governors committing to it
claims.source_outlet: USA TODAY via Central Oregon Daily
claims.notes: Corroborated independently by POWER magazine, see C04. Two independent outlets carry the non binding characterization.

claims.claim: The White House pledge is voluntary and relies on utilities, developers and tech firms to honor nonbinding commitments
claims.verbatim: The White House pledge is voluntary and relies on utilities, developers, and tech firms to honor nonbinding commitments
claims.notes: Trade press. Second independent source for the voluntary framing alongside USA TODAY.

claims.claim: The pledge preamble states that the American people should not be footing the bill for the benefit of private companies
claims.verbatim: As that infrastructure grows and the related electricity demand increases, the American people should not be footing the bill for the benefit of private companies.
claims.notes: Quoted on the RGA page as the pledge text reading in part. Strong cover line.

claims.claim: The pledge sets five commitments for signing companies, build bring or buy new power supply, pay for new power delivery infrastructure, pay whether they use the power or not, invest in local jobs and workforce development, and contribute to grid and community resilience
claims.verbatim: Build, bring, or buy new power supply
claims.notes: Five and only five, read from the White House page. The five headings are rendered as a list. EPA independently describes the same five obligations in prose, confirming the count of five.

claims.claim: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said the global race for AI is underway and America must win it, but not by asking working families to pay for it
claims.verbatim: The global race for AI is underway, and America must win it
claims.notes: The original sentence continues after a dash with the clause but not by asking working families to pay for it. Verbatim span given here is dash free per house style. Quote the two spans joined by a comma on the slide.

claims.claim: The pledge was first signed on March 4, 2026 by seven AI companies and hyperscalers, Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI
claims.verbatim: On March 4, 2026, seven leading AI companies and hyperscalers, Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle, and xAI, signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge at the White House.
claims.notes: Source sentence sets the company list off with dashes; rendered here with commas per house style, wording otherwise unchanged. Corroborated by POWER.

claims.claim: As POWER reported the July 23 expansion, the coalition covered 187 organizations across three stakeholder groups plus 23 governors, made up of 55 investor owned utilities, 105 electric cooperatives and public power entities, 27 data center developers and the seven AI companies
claims.verbatim: 187 organizations across three stakeholder groups, along with 23 governors
claims.notes: CORRECTS the scouts, who reported 56 investor owned utilities, 108 cooperatives and 28 developers. POWER says 55, 105 and 27, which sums to 187. Use this dated set OR C10, never both in the same slide.

claims.claim: Read live on July 26, 2026 the White House signatory page counters showed All 281, Cooperatives 176, Utilities 69 and Data Center Developers 35
claims.verbatim: All 281 Cooperatives 176 Utilities 69 Data Center Developers 35
claims.notes: Two independent fetches returned this identical counter string. CORRECTS the scout, who mis-assigned 35 to developers and dropped a category. Arithmetic flag, 176 plus 69 plus 35 equals 280, not 281, so the All count does not close. Present as the page counter read on 2026-07-26, do not do arithmetic on it on a slide.

claims.claim: Cordova Electric Cooperative is listed as a signatory on the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge page under the Cooperative category
claims.verbatim: Cordova Electric Cooperative / Cooperative / cordovaelectric.com
claims.notes: KILLS the scouts zero Alaska signatories claim. Two separate fetches of the page both returned this row, and the linked domain cordovaelectric.com resolves to the Alaska cooperative, see C12.

claims.claim: Cordova Electric Cooperative is located in Cordova, Alaska
claims.verbatim: Prince William Sounds Science Center, Level 2, 700 New England Cannery Rd, Cordova, AK 99574, United States
claims.notes: Confirms the signatory is the Alaska entity and not a similarly named cooperative in another state.

claims.claim: Cordova Electric Cooperative is the only Alaska entity on the White House signatory list as read on July 26, 2026
claims.verbatim: No other entries contain those Alaska-specific utility names.
claims.notes: Absence claim held to the higher bar. The page rendered a full enumerable list showing 281 of 281 and two independent fetches searched it for Alaska, Chugach, Golden Valley, Matanuska, Homer, Kodiak, Copper Valley, Alyeska, Naknek, Kotzebue, Barrow, Juneau and Fairbanks and returned only Cordova. Slide copy must be hedged as of the list read on July 26, 2026, and must say the Railbelt utilities do not appear rather than asserting they refused.

claims.claim: Cordova Electric Cooperative serves 1,566 customers
claims.verbatim: 1,566 customers
claims.notes: Primary self reported figure. No date shown on the page, so treat as current not as of a stated year.

claims.claim: Cordova is not connected by transmission line to other communities
claims.verbatim: Cordova is not connected to the State Highway System, and CEC is not connected by transmission line to other communities.
claims.notes: Primary. This is the fact that makes the signature symbolically small, the one Alaska signer is not on the grid any Alaska data center would connect to.

claims.claim: Cordova Electric Cooperative has total generating capacity of 18 megawatts across one diesel plant and two hydroelectric plants
claims.verbatim: Generating capacity of 18 megawatts
claims.notes: Components listed on the same page, Orca Diesel Plant 10.8 megawatts, Power Creek Hydroelectric 6 megawatts, Humpback Creek Hydroelectric 1.25 megawatts, which sums to 18.05.

claims.claim: Cordova hosts a small data center that its electric cooperative operates in partnership with Greensparc
claims.verbatim: Cordova hosts a small data center that its electric co-op utility uses in partnership with Greensparc.
claims.notes: Background labeled, outside the 2026-07-16 to 2026-07-26 window. The article calls the utility Cordova Electrical Association and CEA, which is an outlet error, the legal name is Cordova Electric Cooperative, Inc. Use the correct name on the slide.

claims.claim: The Cordova data center uses only 150 kilowatts and as a pilot project could expand to 3 megawatts and become the cooperative's largest customer
claims.verbatim: However, it utilizes only 150 kilowatts and benefits from Cordova Electrical Association's hydroelectric plant. A pilot project, it could expand to be a 3-megawatt facility and CEA's largest customer.
claims.notes: Background labeled. The 3 MW expansion is a projection, hedge as could expand to. Sanity check passes, 3 MW against 18 MW of system capacity is plausible for a largest customer.

claims.claim: SB 250 by Sen. Loki Tobin was titled An Act relating to data centers and relating to utility service for data centers, was introduced February 18, 2026 and was marked dead May 20, 2026
claims.verbatim: An Act relating to data centers; and relating to utility service for data centers.
claims.notes: akleg.gov BASIS pages returned HTTP 403 on every attempt, so this rests on BillTrack50 for dates and on Davis Wright Tremaine for the death. Senate passage date corroborated by DWT as May 16, 2026. No Senate floor vote count could be obtained from any reachable source, so the deck may NOT cite a vote tally.

claims.claim: SB 250 would have required utilities to enter commission approved contracts with data centers so their infrastructure and service costs are borne by the data center operators rather than shifted to other customers
claims.verbatim: that infrastructure and service costs attributable to those facilities are borne by the data center operators rather than being shifted to other customers
claims.notes: Law firm analysis, authors Wendy Kearns, Elyse Sparks and Michael O'Brien. This is the exact policy the pledge promises voluntarily, which is the deck's hinge.

claims.claim: SB 250 passed the Alaska Senate on May 16, 2026 and then died in the House Community and Regional Affairs Committee
claims.verbatim: Following Senate passage, SB 250 was referred to the House Community and Regional Affairs Committee, where it died.
claims.notes: Senate passage date verbatim on the same page, Senate Bill 250 (SB 250) was sent to the Alaska House of Representatives after passing the Senate on May 16, 2026. BillTrack50 independently records Crossed Over 05/16/2026, so two sources agree.

claims.claim: SB 2 by Sen. Shelley Hughes covered disclosure of election related deepfakes and use of artificial intelligence by state agencies, was introduced January 22, 2025, got one recorded hearing on April 29, 2025 and died
claims.verbatim: An Act relating to disclosure of election-related deepfakes; relating to use of artificial intelligence by state agencies; and relating to transfer of data about individuals between state agencies.
claims.notes: Single sourced because akleg.gov returned HTTP 403. Hedge the death date as recorded dead on May 20, 2026 at the end of the session. The one hearing detail is strong, Senate State Affairs, April 29, 2025, 3:30 PM, Beltz 105.

claims.claim: An Alaska provision sponsored by Rep. Sarah Vance prohibiting creation or possession of AI generated child sexual abuse material took effect July 1, 2026
claims.verbatim: Another provision, sponsored by Homer Republican Rep. Sarah Vance, prohibits creating or possessing child sexual abuse material generated using artificial intelligence.
claims.notes: Verified real and dated. The deck may NOT call this Alaska's only AI statute in force, that claim is unverified, see unresolved. The provable adjacent claim is C22, Alaska has no statute governing state agency AI use or election deepfakes because SB 2 died.

claims.claim: Rep. Nick Begich introduced the House DATA Act of 2026 on April 21, 2026 with Reps. Dan Crenshaw and Burgess Owens as a companion to Senate legislation led by Sen. Tom Cotton
claims.verbatim: Senate legislation led by Senator Tom Cotton (R-Ark.)
claims.notes: Background labeled, outside window. The fetch rendered the cosponsor name with a transcription artifact; the correct name is Burgess Owens, R-UT. No H.R. number appears in the release and congress.gov was not reachable, so the deck may NOT cite a bill number.

claims.claim: Begich says the DATA Act allows manufacturers to operate on fully self contained grid of one power systems so innovation can scale without forcing households to subsidize massive new energy demands
claims.verbatim: The DATA Act allows manufacturers to operate on fully self-contained, 'grid-of-one' power systems, so innovation can scale without forcing households to subsidize massive new energy demands or straining local utilities.
claims.notes: Verbatim from the primary press release. Note this is the opposite instrument to SB 250, it protects ratepayers by removing the load from the shared grid rather than by regulating the contract.

claims.claim: The Department of the Air Force is offering approximately 4,700 acres across twelve parcels at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station for potential AI data centers
claims.verbatim: The DAF is offering approximately 4,700 acres of underutilized land across Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base, and Clear Space Force Station.
claims.notes: Background labeled. Parcel count verbatim on the same page, Twelve parcels have been identified for potential development. The scouts proposals due end of June 2026 detail does NOT appear in this article and is killed.

claims.claim: Robert Moriarty, Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Installations, called the land offering a unique opportunity for a true public private partnership supporting the growing demands of the AI industry
claims.verbatim: This is a unique opportunity for a true public-private partnership. By making this land available, we are supporting the growing demands of the AI industry while generating value that directly supports our missions and the readiness of our Airmen and Guardians.
claims.notes: Verbatim quote and exact title confirmed on the primary page.

claims.claim: UAF energy historian Philip Wight said power is the one requirement Alaska is shortest on
claims.verbatim: Power is the one requirement we are shortest on.
claims.notes: Background labeled. Quote appears verbatim on the fetched page. A second Wight line is available if needed, Energy isn't just a small constraint here, it's a major barrier.

claims.claim: The Railbelt can absorb about 25 megawatts and the planned Eielson microreactor is 5 megawatts
claims.verbatim: 25 megawatts of power
claims.notes: Background labeled and March dated, so hedge as reported in March 2026. Both figures appear on the page, the second verbatim is 5-megawatt microreactor. Sanity check, 25 MW of Railbelt headroom against 4,700 acres of offered data center land is the deck's scale contrast and it holds.

claims.claim: Alaska's third special session on the gas line was called by executive proclamation effective July 27, 2026 at 10:00 a.m.
claims.verbatim: the governor has already issued an executive proclamation to call the legislature back into session effective July 27, 2026 at 10:00 a.m.
claims.notes: CORRECTS the scout on publication date, the article is dated July 20, 2026 at 5:20 PM AKDT, not July 21. Juneau is only implied by the article, not stated, so the deck may not assert the location. The article contains NO mention of data centers or AI, which supports the scouts negative finding.

killed.scout_claim: NO Alaska utility, cooperative or developer appears on the White House signatory list.
killed.why_killed: FALSE. Two independent fetches both return a signatory row reading Cordova Electric Cooperative, categorized Cooperative, linking to cordovaelectric.com, which resolves to 700 New England Cannery Rd, Cordova, AK 99574. The scout searched for the string Alaska and missed an Alaska utility whose name does not contain it. Replaced by C11 through C16.

killed.scout_claim: 56 investor-owned utilities, 108 cooperatives, 28 developers at the July 23 expansion.
killed.why_killed: Numbers do not match the cited source. POWER says 55, 105 and 27, which sums to the 187 total the scout also reported. The scout's figures sum to 191. Corrected in C09.

killed.scout_claim: The live White House list reads 281 total with 35 developers.
killed.why_killed: Partially killed. The counter string is confirmed verbatim but the category mapping was wrong and the categories sum to 280 not 281. Survives only as C10, a page counter read on a date, with no arithmetic performed on it.

Could not be verified from any reachable source. akleg.gov, legiscan, trackbill all returned HTTP 403; openstates rendered no bill content. No claim may rest on a failed fetch. The deck may not mention HB 259 in any form.

killed.scout_claim: The Regulatory Commission of Alaska has no open large-load or data-center tariff docket.
killed.why_killed: rca.alaska.gov returned HTTP 403 on both the root and the RCAWeb home page. An absence claim on a regulator's docket cannot rest on a failed fetch. The deck may not claim either way.

Not re-verified this run. The muni.org Assembly page returned no ordinance detail and the ADN article URL returned HTTP 404. Carried over from a prior run without a fetchable source, so it dies under this run's rules.

killed.scout_claim: Alaska has 8 data centers, fourth fewest, against Virginia's 639.
killed.why_killed: No underlying source reachable. Alaska's News Source URL returned HTTP 404 and datacentermap.com returned HTTP 429. Killed entirely.

killed.scout_claim: Air Force EUL proposals due end of June 2026 and no award announced.
killed.why_killed: The deadline does not appear in the fetched af.mil article and the no-award element is an absence claim with no fetched source. Both killed. Acreage, parcel count and the Moriarty quote survive as C26 and C27.
elections.alaska.gov returned HTTP 503 on two different paths. Unverified and not load bearing for this deck.

killed.scout_claim: Chugach Electric's Hilcorp gas contract expires in 2028.
killed.why_killed: No source offered and none found. Killed on sight.

killed.scout_claim: A second Zeldin quote about communities deserving every fact and every protection.
killed.why_killed: A targeted second fetch did not confirm the attribution. Only C07 is confirmed as Zeldin's.

killed.scout_claim: Governors commit to protect American consumers from price hikes due to data center energy.
killed.why_killed: This exact phrasing could not be located on any fetched page. The verified commitment wording is C02.

unresolved.question: Current status of Alaska HB 259.
unresolved.why: akleg.gov BASIS, legiscan and trackbill all returned HTTP 403; openstates rendered no bill data; the DWT analysis does not mention it.
unresolved.what_the_deck_may_say_instead: Say nothing about HB 259. The instrument spine is fully carried by SB 250 and SB 2, both verified dead.

unresolved.question: Does the RCA have any open large load or data center tariff docket?
unresolved.why: rca.alaska.gov returned HTTP 403 on the root and on RCAWeb/Home.aspx.
unresolved.what_the_deck_may_say_instead: Say nothing about RCA dockets in either direction. Use instead the verified fact that SB 250 would have required commission approved contracts and died before creating that authority.

unresolved.question: Is the AI generated CSAM prohibition genuinely Alaska's only AI specific statute in force?
unresolved.why: The ADN article establishes it exists and took effect but never uses the word only, and no statutory survey was reachable.
unresolved.what_the_deck_may_say_instead: Alaska's one AI specific criminal prohibition took effect July 1, 2026, and the bill that would have governed state agency AI use and election deepfakes, SB 2, died without a second hearing. Both halves are verified.

unresolved.question: Has DNR issued a final decision on STAK Energy's North Slope lease ADL 422741?
unresolved.why: dnr.alaska.gov public notice path returned HTTP 404 and no alternate source was reachable.
unresolved.what_the_deck_may_say_instead: Docket entry only, marked status unverified this run. Do not state a decision either way.

unresolved.question: Was there a Senate floor vote count on SB 250?
unresolved.why: Every Alaska legislature source 403d. BillTrack50 records the crossover date but carries no tally.
unresolved.what_the_deck_may_say_instead: SB 250 passed the Alaska Senate on May 16, 2026. Do not cite a vote count.

unresolved.question: How many data centers does Alaska have?
unresolved.why: Both candidate sources returned HTTP 404 and HTTP 429.
unresolved.what_the_deck_may_say_instead: Use the verified Cordova figures instead, a 150 kilowatt pilot in a town whose entire utility has 18 MW of generation.

verdict: Yes, and it is a materially better deck than the one the scouts pitched. The original spine, a signature with zero Alaska signatories behind it, was factually wrong and was killed. The verified replacement is sharper. The weakest link is C13, the only Alaska entity claim, an absence assertion resting on two reads of one page, which must be dated on the slide as of the White House list read on July 26, 2026. The second weakest is C10, the 281 counter, whose categories sum to 280, so it must be shown as a counter and never as arithmetic. Do not let HB 259, the RCA docket, Anchorage AO 2026-27, the eight data centers figure or the Air Force proposal deadline onto any slide.
